opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
After Jesus’ death, the disciples didn’t disappear—they went to work. Not by their own strength, but through the Holy Spirit that Jesus gave them. It was through that Spirit that they performed what seemed impossible.
And that same Spirit has been given to us.
At Confirmation, we accepted that same gift—the same power, the same presence. The question is not whether we have it. The question is whether we live from it.
Scripture says, “there is no other name under heaven… by which we are saved,” So how do we actually live that?  It starts with understanding what Jesus has already done.  His birth, His life, His death–none of it was random.  It was intentional. He reconciled sinners to the Father completely.  That work is finished.  The outcome is already secured, and you are not trying to earn anything.  

“This is the day the Lord has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it” (Psalms 118) stops being a nice line and becomes a way of living. Every day is no longer something we control or carry alone, but something given.

Once that is in place, joy shows up, but not as something you chase. Joy is the byproduct, not the goal. It comes from clarity about Christ, trust in His control, and surrender of your need to control outcomes. When that is real, the joy becomes steady, not emotional spikes, and it becomes visible. People feel it. It draws them. That is evangelization in its pure form—not arguing, not forcing, but being anchored in something others don’t have. And this is where honesty matters. You don’t do this halfway. If you are still relying on control, still chasing validation, still measuring your life by outcomes, the joy will not sustain. The real shift happens when you let go of the illusion that your life is yours to manage completely. That is where the Spirit actually becomes active.

And then there’s this moment in the Gospel of John that seems oddly specific. After the resurrection, the disciples go fishing. They catch nothing on their own. Jesus tells them where to cast the net—and suddenly they pull in 153 large fish, and yet the net is not torn.
Why so specific?
First, it shows this actually happened. Someone counted them. This is eyewitness detail.  But the early Church also saw something deeper. The number 153 was believed to represent the fullness of all fish—meaning all nations, all people. The net represents the Church, and the fact that it was not torn shows that what Christ builds can hold the weight of that mission.

And there’s another layer:
The disciples worked all night and caught nothing. Only when they followed Jesus did the abundance come. That’s the pattern. Effort alone leads to emptiness. Effort aligned with Christ leads to fullness. And not chaotic fullness—ordered, sustained, intentional abundance.
That connects directly to us.
When we try to control everything, strive for everything, and carry everything—we come up empty or exhausted. But when we live from what Christ has already done—when we actually trust it—there is a different result.
Peace.
Stability.
And yes, joy.
